stem: A 50-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to severe, constant upper abdominal pain and vomiting for the past 8 hours.  She has had several prior episodes of similar abdominal pain that resolved spontaneously without treatment.  Her temperature is 37.8 C (100 F) and pulse is 112/min.  Abdominal examination shows cessation of inspiration with deep palpation of the right upper quadrant.  Which of the following findings would be most specific for acute cholecystitis?​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​

options.label: C
options.text: Increased serum aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels

options.label: E
options.text: Persistent failure of bile to enter the gallbladder

explanation:
Acute cholecystitis and biliary colic are most often caused by gallstone obstruction of the cystic duct.  Fatty foods stimulate cholecystokinin release, and the resulting gallbladder contraction against the obstructing stone causes severe, constant pain.

Biliary colic results from transient obstruction and resolves within a few hours once the stone dislodges.  In contrast, persistent obstruction in acute cholecystitis causes pain lasting >6 hours.  The prolonged increase in intraluminal pressure causes injury to the gallbladder mucosa; released phospholipases convert biliary lecithin to lysolecithin, a mucosal toxin, and prostaglandins further amplify inflammation.

Gallstones are common in adults and usually asymptomatic, so their presence establishes only cholelithiasis.  More specific findings include signs of gallbladder inflammation or evidence of persistent cystic duct obstruction, which prevents bile from entering the gallbladder.

Ultrasonography is the preferred initial imaging test for suspected acute cholecystitis because it can identify associated inflammatory findings (eg, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign).  When ultrasonography is inconclusive, hepatobiliary scintigraphy (cholescintigraphy, hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid [HIDA] scan) can directly assess cystic duct patency.

During a hepatobiliary scan, an intravenous radiotracer is taken up by hepatocytes (panel A) and excreted into bile.  With a patent cystic duct, the radiotracer accumulates in the gallbladder, which becomes visible (panel C, arrow).  In acute cholecystitis, tracer passes through the common bile duct into the proximal small bowel, but the gallbladder is not visualized, even on delayed images, because the persistently obstructed cystic duct prevents bile from entering (panel B, arrow).

(Choice A)  A distended duodenum suggests proximal intestinal obstruction or localized ileus from adjacent inflammation (eg, pancreatitis); it is not specific for gallbladder inflammation.

(Choice B)  Most cases of acute cholecystitis are caused by gallstones, but the presence of gallstones does not indicate gallbladder inflammation.  Cholelithiasis can also cause more benign biliary colic (likely the cause of this patient's prior episodes) or be an incidental asymptomatic finding.

(Choice C)  Mild increases in serum aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels can occur in acute cholecystitis, but they are nonspecific markers of hepatocellular injury and do not localize disease to the gallbladder.

(Choice D)  Leukocytosis with increased band neutrophils (left shift) reflects the systemic response to acute inflammation or infection.  It is common in acute cholecystitis but also occurs with many other causes of acute abdominal pain (eg, appendicitis, pancreatitis, pyelonephritis).

Educational objective:Acute cholecystitis is most often caused by gallstones obstructing the cystic duct.  Because gallstones are common and often asymptomatic, their presence does not establish the diagnosis, which requires signs of gallbladder inflammation (eg, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid) or evidence of persistent cystic duct obstruction (eg, gallbladder nonvisualization on hepatobiliary scintigraphy).​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​
